chief_complaint: shivering chills, yellow skin, and right upper side stomach pain for 24 hours
hpi_details: Presents to ER with acute 24-hour history of severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain accompanied by high spiking fevers, violent rigors/shivering, and rapidly developing jaundice. Patient appears unwell, drowsy, and slightly confused according to his son. Has a known history of gallstones but declined elective surgery 2 years ago.
ideas: son thinks a gallstone has completely blocked the bile pipe and caused severe poisoning
concerns: son is terrified his father is going into septic shock
expectations: wants immediate IV antibiotics and an emergency procedure to clear the blockage
pmh: cholelithiasis diagnosed on ultrasound 2 years ago, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension
social_hx: retired shop owner, non-smoker, rare alcohol intake

investigation_events.title: STAT ascending cholangitis results
investigation_events.availability_message: The STAT sepsis, liver, and biliary ultrasound results are now available; cultures, antibiotics, fluids, and urgent biliary decompression should not be delayed.

results.value: Dilated common bile duct measuring 12 mm with an obstructing distal duct stone and intrahepatic biliary dilatation; gallstones present

clinical_knowledge.topic: Acute Ascending Cholangitis evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Ascending Cholangitis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Medical/surgical emergency: Sepsis 6 resuscitation (IV crystalloids, high-flow O2 if hypoxic, blood cultures prior to antibiotics, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem, monitor lactate/urine output), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: shivering chills, yellow skin, and right upper side stomach pain for 24 hours

Key HPI features: Presents to ER with acute 24-hour history of severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain accompanied by high spiking fevers, violent rigors/shivering, and rapidly developing jaundice. Patient appears unwell, drowsy, and slightly confused according to his son. Has a known history of gallstones but declined elective surgery 2 years ago.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: temperature 39.1°C, HR 114, BP 92/58, RR 24. Abdominal exam: tender RUQ with guarding. Scleral icterus visible. Bloods: FBC (neutrophilia), blood cultures x2 sets, LFTs (obstructive pattern: raised bilirubin and ALP > ALT), CRP, urea/creatinine, lactate. Urgent abdominal ultrasound or CT abdomen, progressing to ERCP.
Relevant background/PMH: cholelithiasis diagnosed on ultrasound 2 years ago, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension
Current medications: metformin 850mg BD, ramipril 5mg OD
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Ascending Cholangitis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Acute suppurative cholecystitis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Confusion or drowsiness with fever and jaundice — suggests progression to septic shock (Reynolds pentad).
management_principles: Medical/surgical emergency: Sepsis 6 resuscitation (IV crystalloids, high-flow O2 if hypoxic, blood cultures prior to antibiotics, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem, monitor lactate/urine output)
Urgent gastroenterology/surgical consult for emergency biliary decompression via Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with sphincterotomy/stenting within 24 hours
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 66M with known gallstones presents with Charcot's triad (RUQ pain, fever/rigors, jaundice) progressing toward Reynolds' pentad (plus confusion and hypotension).
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: temperature 39.1°C, HR 114, BP 92/58, RR 24. Abdominal exam: tender RUQ with guarding. Scleral icterus visible. Bloods: FBC (neutrophilia), blood cultures x2 sets, LFTs (obstructive pattern: raised bilirubin and ALP > ALT), CRP, urea/creatinine, lactate. Urgent abdominal ultrasound or CT abdomen, progressing to ERCP.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute ascending cholangitis (biliary sepsis) likely secondary to choledocholithiasis. DDx: acute suppurative cholecystitis, liver abscess, severe viral/drug hepatitis, mirizzi syndrome.
reference_soap.plan: Medical/surgical emergency: Sepsis 6 resuscitation (IV crystalloids, high-flow O2 if hypoxic, blood cultures prior to antibiotics, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem, monitor lactate/urine output). Urgent gastroenterology/surgical consult for emergency biliary decompression via Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with sphincterotomy/stenting within 24 hours.

learning_objectives: Identify Charcot's triad (RUQ pain, fever, jaundice) and Reynolds' pentad indicating life-threatening ascending cholangitis
Recognise the obstructive LFT profile (predominant alkaline phosphatase and conjugated bilirubin elevation)
Execute immediate sepsis resuscitation and blood culture acquisition before antibiotic initiation
Explain the urgent necessity of mechanical biliary decompression via ERCP alongside antibiotic therapy

teaching.one_liner: A gallstone blocks the bile duct and bacteria multiply upstream, causing the classic triad of right-upper-quadrant pain, fever with rigors, and jaundice — a biliary sepsis emergency.
red_flags: Confusion or drowsiness with fever and jaundice — suggests progression to septic shock (Reynolds pentad)

must_ask.say: Have you had pain, fevers with shivering, and yellow skin all together?
Has your father seemed confused or unusually drowsy?
Has he been told before that he has gallstones?
Did he ever have an operation offered for the gallstones, and why wasn't it done?
Has his urine gone darker, or his stools become pale?
Did he have violent shaking or shivering with the fever?

history.answer: I feel burning hot with terrible shaking chills, my right belly hurts badly, and my son says my eyes and skin turned yellow since yesterday.
The high fever began abruptly yesterday morning, about 24 hours ago, and has stayed high since.
My temperature shot up over 39 degrees, and I had violent shivering spells that made my whole body shake and teeth chatter.
My son gave me two acetaminophen tablets earlier today, but they barely brought the fever down at all.
No, I haven't had any cough, phlegm, sore throat, or shortness of breath.
I don't have any pain or burning when I urinate, and my flanks don't hurt, though my urine has turned as dark as iced tea.
My bowel movement yesterday looked strangely pale and clay-colored, but I haven't had any diarrhea.
It is a constant, severe aching and squeezing pain in my upper right stomach that has steadily worsened since yesterday.
I have been very nauseated and vomited stomach fluid once yesterday evening, but there was no blood in it.
I have a dull headache from the burning fever, but my neck does not feel stiff or painful to move.
I feel very sluggish and drowsy today, and my son noticed I was speaking somewhat confusedly and forgetting things earlier.
No, I have no rash, hives, purple spots, or insect bites with dark scabs anywhere.
No, none of my joints are swollen, red, or aching.
No drenching night sweats before this began yesterday, and my weight has been completely steady.
No, I haven't noticed any swollen glands or lumps in my neck, armpits, or groin.
No, I have not traveled abroad, gone hiking in tall grass, worked on a farm, or handled any animals.
No, nobody in my family or neighborhood has been sick with a fever or stomach bug.
No, I have never had cancer treatment, chemotherapy, steroids, or any immunosuppressive drugs.
No, I don't have an artificial heart valve or heart murmur, and I haven't had any dental work done recently.
No, I haven't started any new prescription drugs, over-the-counter painkillers, or herbal tonics lately.
I have been in a monogamous marriage for decades, and I have never injected illicit drugs.
I have had high blood pressure and type 2 diabetes for about ten years.
An ultrasound two years ago showed I had gallstones after I had an episode of stomach cramps.
The surgeon advised me to remove my gallbladder two years ago, but I declined because my symptoms had settled down.
I take metformin 850 milligrams twice daily for my sugar and ramipril 5 milligrams once daily for my blood pressure.
I have no known allergies to any medications or antibiotics.
I have never smoked cigarettes or tobacco in my life.
I almost never drink alcohol, perhaps just half a glass of beer on a rare special occasion once or twice a year.
I am a retired convenience store owner, and I live at home with my wife and adult son.
My father had high blood pressure, but there is no family history of liver disease, jaundice, or gallbladder trouble.
My son is terrified that a loose gallstone has completely blocked my bile duct and caused severe blood poisoning.

exam.finding: Ill-appearing, flushed, diaphoretic, lethargic, and mildly confused.
Temperature 39.1°C, heart rate 114 bpm, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths/min, SpO2 95% on ambient air.
Marked scleral icterus bilaterally with normal pink conjunctivae.
Mucous membranes are dry; pharynx and tonsils are clear without erythema or exudate.
No anterior or posterior cervical lymphadenopathy palpable.
Clear vesicular breath sounds bilaterally with no crackles, wheezes, or pleural friction rubs.
Tachycardic regular rhythm with distinct S1 and S2; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops heard.
Flat abdomen with noticeable cutaneous jaundice; no distension, caput medusae, or surgical scars.
Hypoactive bowel sounds audible throughout all four quadrants.
Marked tenderness and involuntary guarding in the right upper quadrant; remainder of abdomen is soft.
Sharp arrest of inspiration upon palpation beneath the right costal margin.
Liver edge is palpable two centimeters below the costal margin and tender; spleen is not palpable.
No costovertebral angle tenderness on gentle percussion bilaterally.
Deep jaundice across the torso and limbs with no petechiae, purpura, rash, or eschar.
Neck is supple with full passive flexion; Kernig and Brudzinski signs are absent.
